    3. collagen metabolic process (GO:0032963)

    Agent Summary: The collagen metabolic process involves a series of steps including synthesis, modification, and degradation of collagen, which is crucial for maintaining the structural integrity of blood vessels and organs involved in blood pressure regulation. Core family members: COL1A1, COL5A1, CST3, CTSB, CTSL, CTSS. [244] [245] [246]
    Read Context ▽

    The collagen metabolic process comprises the synthesis, post-translational modification, assembly, cross-linking, deposition, remodeling, and degradation of collagen, the principal structural protein of the extracellular matrix in connective tissues. Collagen provides tensile strength and mechanical stability to blood vessels, myocardium, and other organs that are critically involved in blood pressure regulation and target-organ injury. This pathway includes intracellular biosynthetic steps such as procollagen production and hydroxylation of proline residues, extracellular fibril formation, and dynamic turnover mediated by proteases and their inhibitors. In vascular and cardiac tissues, balanced collagen metabolism is essential for preserving wall compliance, elasticity, and normal cell-matrix signaling. Disturbance of this balance can lead either to excessive collagen accumulation, which promotes fibrosis and stiffening, or to abnormal collagen proteolysis, which alters mechanotransduction and stimulates maladaptive cellular responses. The publications provided indicate that collagen metabolism is tightly regulated by oxidative stress, inflammation, immune activation, transforming growth factor beta-related and independent profibrotic signaling, aldosterone-related signaling, epigenetic mechanisms, and matrix metalloproteinase activity. Thus, collagen metabolism is not merely a passive structural pathway, but may be considered a central effector of vascular remodeling, myocardial fibrosis, microvascular dysfunction, and altered arterial mechanics.

    Against this biological background, the collected literature supports a pathogenic association between dysregulated collagen metabolism and hypertension through vascular fibrosis, arterial stiffening, microvascular remodeling, and cardiac injury. A central theme is that oxidative stress initiates immune and fibrotic responses that increase vascular collagen deposition; in mice with excessive vascular reactive oxygen species production, collagen accumulation in the aorta was accompanied by aortic stiffening, renal dysfunction, and hypertension, and these abnormalities depended on T lymphocyte activation and were prevented by scavenging oxidative products, indicating that collagen deposition is likely to be a mechanistic component rather than a secondary byproduct of elevated pressure alone [244]. Consistent with this concept, studies of resistance vessels in essential hypertension showed earlier and more extensive collagen fiber deposition together with oxidative stress and structural remodeling than in physiological aging, supporting the view that hypertension accelerates profibrotic extracellular matrix remodeling [245]. Collagen metabolic imbalance in hypertension also involves altered degradation. In early renovascular hypertension, increased matrix metalloproteinase two activity promoted type one collagen proteolysis, which activated focal adhesion kinase signaling and vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, thereby contributing to hypertrophic remodeling of the aortic wall; this observation suggests that both excess collagen deposition and abnormal collagen breakdown can drive hypertensive vascular pathology through distinct mechanisms [246]. Beyond the systemic vasculature, pulmonary vascular disease provides complementary evidence that collagen metabolism is directly linked to hypertensive remodeling: neural precursor cell expressed developmentally down-regulated nine promoted collagen type three alpha one expression, increased endothelial stiffness, and enhanced collagen one and collagen three accumulation in pulmonary vascular cells, while its inhibition prevented fibrotic remodeling and pulmonary arterial hypertension in vivo [247]. Similarly, right ventricular fibroblasts in experimental pulmonary arterial hypertension exhibited a persistent metabolic program that increased collagen production and fibrosis, and pharmacological reversal of this program reduced fibrosis and improved function, further connecting collagen synthesis to hypertensive end-organ damage [248]. Cardiac studies in systemic hypertension also reinforce this relationship, as inhibition of deoxyribonucleic acid methylation reduced collagen one and collagen three expression, myocardial fibrosis, and hypertrophy in spontaneously hypertensive rats, indicating that epigenetic control of collagen metabolism contributes to pressure-induced cardiac remodeling [249]. Clinical and translational observations align with these experimental findings: patients with arterial hypertension exhibit increased myocardial interstitial collagen and elevated circulating markers of collagen formation and fibrosis, which can be attenuated by antihypertensive therapy with antifibrotic properties [250], while recent reviews identify excessive collagen deposition as a core feature of hypertensive microvascular dysfunction that increases vascular resistance and promotes injury in the heart, kidney, brain, and retina [251]. Collectively, these studies indicate that the collagen metabolic process is fundamentally involved in hypertension because it translates oxidative, inflammatory, hormonal, metabolic, and mechanical stress into structural remodeling of vessels and myocardium, thereby increasing stiffness, impairing vasodilation, promoting maladaptive cell proliferation, and sustaining target-organ damage. [244] [245] [246] [247] [248] [249] [250] [251]

    To further contextualize these 18 proteins, the interaction network offers a complementary view of how these molecules may be functionally connected within the broader collagen remodeling landscape. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 18 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network inspection and further interaction-based interpretation.

    MMP8 stands out as the protein with the clearest potential relevance to hypertension because its collagenolytic activity directly implicates extracellular matrix remodeling. By degrading fibrillar collagens, MMP8 may influence the structural integrity and turnover of the vascular wall, a process that is highly relevant to hypertension, where arterial stiffening, fibrosis, and maladaptive remodeling are central pathophysiological features. Altered collagen balance in resistance arteries and large vessels contributes to increased vascular stiffness and elevated peripheral resistance, both of which promote blood pressure elevation. Therefore, proteins such as MMP8 that regulate collagen degradation may participate in either adaptive remodeling or pathological matrix disruption, depending on context. Although no citation was provided in the input for this function, the biological role itself supports MMP8 as a plausible contributor to hypertension-associated vascular remodeling.

    In a related but distinct way, VSIR is notable because it links two mechanisms increasingly recognized in hypertension: immune dysregulation and matrix remodeling. Its reported role as an immunoregulatory receptor that inhibits T-cell responses suggests potential relevance to the inflammatory component of hypertension, as activated T cells and low-grade vascular inflammation are known to contribute to endothelial dysfunction, vascular injury, and sustained blood pressure elevation. In this context, VSIR could influence disease susceptibility or progression by modulating the magnitude of adaptive immune activation. In addition, the reported ability of VSIR to stimulate MMP14-mediated MMP2 activation provides a second mechanistic connection to hypertension, since MMP2 is implicated in vascular extracellular matrix turnover, arterial remodeling, and fibrosis. These combined immune and proteolytic functions make VSIR particularly interesting as a candidate regulator at the intersection of inflammation and structural vascular change in hypertensive disease. The BMP4-related annotation may also be relevant indirectly, because BMP signaling has recognized roles in vascular biology, although the strongest hypertension-related implications here derive from T-cell inhibition and MMP2 pathway activation. [252] [253]

    By contrast, PRSS2 does not stand out in the present dataset because no functional annotation was provided from which to infer a meaningful connection to hypertension. Without a defined role in vascular biology, inflammation, extracellular matrix regulation, renal sodium handling, or neurohormonal signaling, its relevance to hypertension cannot be evaluated on the basis of the supplied information alone.

    4. regulation of blood pressure (GO:0008217)

    Agent Summary: The regulation of blood pressure involves a complex interplay between various physiological systems, including the kidneys, vasculature, heart, nervous system, and endocrine and immune signals, alongside environmental factors like dietary sodium and gut microb Pathway members (enrichment overlap): ACE, ACE2, ACVRL1, ADM, CALCA, CHGA. Context proteins (upstream regulators / disease context, not direct members): IL6, KDR, TGFB1, VEGFA. [227] [228] [229]
    Read Context ▽

    Regulation of blood pressure comprises the integrated physiological processes that determine the force exerted by circulating blood on the arterial wall. This pathway is maintained through dynamic interactions among the kidney, vasculature, heart, nervous system, endocrine signals, immune mechanisms, and environmental inputs such as dietary sodium and microbial metabolites. Under normal conditions, blood pressure is stabilized by balancing mechanisms that increase vascular tone, cardiac output, and sodium and water retention against mechanisms that promote vasodilation, natriuresis, and volume reduction. The publications provided suggest that this pathway extends beyond classical hemodynamic control and includes tissue sodium storage, renal tubular sodium transport, endothelial vasoactive mediators, arterial stiffness, autonomic regulation, circadian blood pressure patterning, sex-dependent hormonal modulation, gut microbiota, and immune-inflammatory signaling. In particular, sodium handling by the kidney and extrarenal tissues, including non-osmotic sodium storage in skin and muscle, has emerged as a potentially important determinant of blood pressure homeostasis. Renal sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb through sodium potassium two chloride cotransporter activity also appears to represent a key component of long-term blood pressure control. At the vascular level, endothelial balance between nitric oxide and endothelin one influences vasoconstriction, oxidative stress, inflammation, vascular remodeling, and arterial stiffening. In parallel, the gut microbiota may contribute to blood pressure regulation through production of short-chain fatty acids and other metabolites that act on host receptors, alter immune tone, and influence sympathetic outflow through the gut-brain axis. Taken together, regulation of blood pressure can be viewed as a multi-organ and multi-scale pathway whose disruption may contribute to the initiation, maintenance, and complications of hypertension.

    This broader disease context is also consistent with the enrichment results obtained for the present protein set. There were 21 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway regulating blood pressure, a complex multi-organ process that integrates renal sodium handling, vascular tone control, cardiac output regulation, autonomic signaling, endocrine modulation, immune-inflammatory activity, tissue sodium storage, circadian variation, sex-dependent hormonal effects, and microbial metabolite signaling. This enrichment is biologically consistent with hypertension because sustained elevation of arterial pressure emerges when the quantitative balance shifts toward greater vasoconstriction, higher sodium and water retention, increased arterial stiffness, enhanced sympathetic drive, and amplified inflammatory signaling, while counter-regulatory processes such as vasodilation, natriuresis, and volume reduction become insufficient. In this context, the identified protein set maps to a pathway in which the kidney, vasculature, heart, nervous system, immune system, and gut collectively determine blood pressure homeostasis, thereby supporting the relevance of all 21 proteins to hypertension pathogenesis and progression. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 21 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for direct network inspection.

    To further clarify how this enrichment may relate to hypertension biology, the most significant proteins are discussed below in the same functional context. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

    ACVRL1 is among the most compelling proteins in this list with respect to hypertension because it directly regulates endothelial signaling and angiogenesis, two processes central to vascular tone, arterial remodeling, and peripheral resistance. Its dependence on endoglin and SMAD1 places it within the transforming growth factor beta and bone morphogenetic protein signaling axis, which is well known to influence vascular integrity and endothelial homeostasis. Dysregulation of endothelial growth control can contribute to maladaptive vascular remodeling, rarefaction, and impaired vasodilatory capacity, all of which are mechanistically linked to elevated blood pressure. Moreover, the ACVRL1-endoglin pathway has established relevance to vascular disease states characterized by abnormal vessel structure and hemodynamics, making this protein particularly important when considering hypertension as a disorder of both vascular function and remodeling.

    Consistent with this emphasis on vascular development and endothelial regulation, DLL1 appears to highlight a related but distinct signaling layer. DLL1 stands out strongly because its functions intersect directly with vascular development, arterial specification, angiogenesis, and blood pressure regulation. The Notch pathway is a major determinant of vascular patterning and smooth muscle-endothelial communication, and the description explicitly notes roles in maintaining arterial identity and regulating blood pressure and energy homeostasis. Through its effects on KDR and VEGFA signaling and tip-cell differentiation, DLL1 may influence microvascular architecture and vessel responsiveness, which are relevant to systemic vascular resistance. In addition, Notch signaling has broad effects on tissue remodeling and cell fate decisions in the vasculature, suggesting that altered DLL1 activity could contribute not only to developmental vascular abnormalities but also to adult vascular dysfunction that predisposes to hypertension. Because the provided annotation explicitly connects DLL1 to blood pressure regulation, it is one of the most directly relevant candidates in this dataset. [241] [242]

    Beyond vascular patterning, inflammatory and hemostatic signaling may provide an additional mechanistic bridge to hypertension. F2R is highly relevant to hypertension because it links coagulation, vascular signaling, inflammation, and calcium-dependent cellular responses. Thrombin receptor activation can alter endothelial and vascular cell behavior through intracellular calcium mobilization, a fundamental mechanism in vasomotor regulation and vascular reactivity. Particularly important is the annotation that F2R mediates induction of MCP-1, CCL2, and IL6, inflammatory mediators that are frequently elevated in vascular inflammation and hypertensive target-organ injury. Its roles in platelet activation and vascular development further support a contribution to vascular dysfunction and pro-thrombotic states, both of which commonly accompany hypertension. Thus, F2R may be mechanistically connected to hypertension through inflammatory vascular remodeling, endothelial activation, and altered hemostatic signaling. [243]

    A related extension of this theme is provided by GAS6, which may connect endothelial resilience with thrombotic susceptibility. GAS6 is a notable hypertension-related candidate because it integrates endothelial survival signaling with platelet activation and thrombosis-related pathways. The GAS6 and AXL axis is particularly important in vascular biology, where it can preserve endothelial viability under stress conditions and influence vascular remodeling, inflammation, and thrombotic susceptibility. These functions are relevant to hypertension, which is frequently accompanied by endothelial dysfunction, arterial injury, and increased cardiovascular risk. The annotation highlighting regulation of thrombotic responses and platelet activation further strengthens its relevance, as hypertensive vascular disease often coexists with a pro-thrombotic state. Therefore, GAS6 may contribute to hypertension not necessarily as a primary blood pressure regulator, but as an important modulator of vascular resilience and downstream cardiovascular complications.

    In addition to these endothelial and thrombo-inflammatory factors, proteins linked to structural homeostasis of major effector organs also warrant attention. Although the functional annotation for SCPEP1 is relatively brief, it is still potentially important in hypertension because it implicates two organ systems central to blood pressure control: the vasculature and the kidney. Vascular wall homeostasis is directly related to arterial stiffness, remodeling, and resistance vessel function, whereas kidney homeostasis is fundamental for sodium balance, extracellular fluid volume, and long-term blood pressure regulation. Even in the absence of a detailed mechanistic description, a protein associated with both vascular and renal integrity deserves attention in the context of hypertension, particularly as these are the principal effector organs in hypertensive pathophysiology.

    Finally, oxidative balance provides another plausible layer through which the enriched protein set may influence blood pressure regulation. SOD2 is highly relevant to hypertension because oxidative stress is a well-established driver of endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, and impaired nitric oxide bioavailability. By detoxifying mitochondrial superoxide, SOD2 limits reactive oxygen species accumulation that would otherwise promote vasoconstriction, vascular stiffening, and hypertensive end-organ damage. Mitochondrial redox imbalance has been implicated in both the initiation and maintenance of elevated blood pressure, particularly in the vasculature, kidney, and heart. Therefore, SOD2 represents an important protective factor whose reduced activity or increased demand could contribute to the oxidative component of hypertension pathogenesis.

    5. Signaling by Interleukins (REAC:R-HSA-449147)

    Agent Summary: The 'Signaling by Interleukins' pathway plays a crucial role in coordinating immune responses and maintaining tissue homeostasis, with significant implications for hypertension. Core family members: IL10RB, IL12B, IL15, IL15RA, IL16, IL17C. Context proteins (upstream regulators / disease context, not direct members): NOS3. [212] [213] [214]
    Read Context ▽

    Signaling by interleukins comprises a broad cytokine communication network that coordinates innate immunity, adaptive immunity, tissue homeostasis, vascular responses, and repair. Interleukins are secreted predominantly by leukocytes, but also by endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells, epithelial cells, and tissue-resident macrophages, and they act through cognate receptors that activate intracellular cascades such as janus kinase and signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling, nuclear factor kappa B signaling, mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, and inflammasome-associated pathways. Depending on the ligand, receptor context, and target cell, interleukin signaling can promote leukocyte recruitment, differentiation of T helper cell subsets, endothelial activation, oxidative stress, smooth muscle migration and proliferation, barrier dysfunction, and cytokine amplification loops. In cardiovascular disease, this pathway is especially important because it links environmental and hemodynamic stressors, including excess dietary salt, hypoxia, infection, and sleep-disordered breathing, to vascular remodeling, neuroimmune activation, and end-organ injury. The publications provided highlight several interleukin-centered modules relevant to hypertension, including interleukin seventeen signaling from meningeal or gut-derived T cells, interleukin six signaling through glycoprotein one hundred thirty and soluble interleukin six receptor-dependent trans-signaling, interleukin one beta generation through inflammasome activation, and interleukin fifteen deficiency associated with impaired natural killer cell homeostasis. Collectively, these studies position interleukin signaling as a mechanistic bridge between immune dysregulation and the vascular, pulmonary, cerebral, and behavioral complications of hypertension.

    Against this biological background, the collected studies further suggest that signaling by interleukins is not merely a correlate of hypertension but may function as a mechanistic driver of disease initiation, vascular remodeling, and organ damage across systemic and pulmonary forms of hypertension. In salt-sensitive and neurogenic hypertension, excess salt and related inflammatory cues promote T cell polarization toward interleukin seventeen-producing phenotypes, and this cytokine appears to mediate both blood pressure elevation and target-organ injury. In obstructive sleep apnea-induced hypertension, interleukin seventeen neutralization reduced blood pressure and reversed gut and brain inflammation, supporting a causal role for the interleukin seventeen axis in hypertensive neuroimmune dysfunction [212], while in salt-sensitive hypertension, meningeal T cell-derived interleukin seventeen acted on brain border-associated macrophages to cause neurovascular dysfunction and cognitive impairment independent of the degree of blood pressure elevation, suggesting that interleukin signaling may also contribute directly to hypertensive complications [213]. A complementary line of evidence implicates interleukin six as a central mediator of immune and vascular remodeling responses. Single-cell transcriptomics in a salt-sensitive hypertension model showed that a high-salt diet increased interleukin six receptor, janus kinase one, and signal transducer and activator of transcription three pathway activity in intestinal B cells and T follicular helper-like cells, suggesting that gut immune activation may represent an upstream component of hypertension pathogenesis [214]. In pulmonary hypertension, multiple studies converged on pathogenic interleukin six signaling: glycoprotein one hundred thirty deletion in cluster of differentiation four-positive T cells ameliorated hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension and suppressed signal transducer and activator of transcription three activation and T helper seventeen expansion, indicating that interleukin six signaling in helper T cells may drive disease [215]; soluble interleukin six receptor-dependent trans-signaling promoted pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cell migration and chronic hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension, identifying a specific pro-inflammatory interleukin six signaling mode linked to vascular remodeling [216]; and endothelial studies showed that exaggerated interleukin six signaling sustains endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition-like responses and couples oxidative stress to smooth muscle proliferation, further supporting a direct vascular role for this pathway [217] [218]. Interleukin one beta also emerges as an important effector downstream of danger sensing and inflammasome activation. Platelet mitochondrial dysfunction in pulmonary arterial hypertension activated the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like receptor family pyrin domain containing three inflammasome and increased interleukin one beta release, which induced endothelial dysfunction, whereas high salt directly triggered vascular smooth muscle oxidative stress, poly adenosine diphosphate-ribose polymerase and transient receptor potential melastatin two activation, inflammasome assembly, and interleukin one beta and interleukin eighteen production, linking salt excess to vascular injury and elevated blood pressure (PMID not available for platelet study; PubMed:40312994). Additional support for the clinical relevance of interleukin-driven inflammation comes from observational evidence that latent tuberculosis infection, a condition marked by chronic interleukin-rich inflammatory signaling, is associated with increased incident hypertension [219]. Finally, not all interleukin signals are pathogenic in the same direction: impaired interleukin fifteen signaling secondary to bone morphogenetic protein receptor type two loss worsened pulmonary hypertension by reducing natural killer cell homeostasis, showing that loss of protective interleukin circuits can also favor hypertensive vascular disease [220]. Overall, the pathway is related to hypertension through several integrated mechanisms, including immune cell activation and polarization, cytokine amplification, endothelial dysfunction, vascular smooth muscle migration and remodeling, neuroinflammation, and end-organ injury, making interleukin signaling a biologically coherent and therapeutically relevant framework for understanding hypertension. [212] [213] [214] [215] [216] [217] [218] [221] [219] [220]

    Consistent with these literature-based observations, the enrichment results indicate that this pathway captures a substantial hypertension-relevant functional module. There were 53 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway Signaling by interleukins, indicating that this immune communication program may connect inflammatory signaling with vascular, cerebral, pulmonary, and end-organ pathobiology. This enrichment is biologically coherent because interleukin-mediated signaling regulates endothelial activation, leukocyte recruitment, oxidative stress, smooth muscle proliferation, tissue remodeling, and cytokine amplification, all of which are central processes in hypertension progression and complication development. Within this 53-protein set, the pathway description highlights several quantitatively important interleukin-centered axes, including interleukin seventeen signaling, interleukin six signaling through glycoprotein one hundred thirty and soluble interleukin six receptor-dependent trans-signaling, interleukin one beta production driven by inflammasome activation, and interleukin fifteen deficiency linked to disrupted natural killer cell homeostasis. Together, these observations support the interpretation that multiple distinct but convergent inflammatory circuits are represented in the enriched protein group. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 53 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for interactive inspection.

    To further clarify how this enriched set may relate to hypertension biology, the function enrichment analysis identified several proteins of particular interest. We introduce them in detail below. VEGFA stands out as the protein with the most direct and biologically compelling connection to hypertension because its annotated functions converge on endothelial homeostasis, vascular remodeling, and nitric oxide signaling, all of which are core determinants of blood pressure regulation. The described ability to promote endothelial proliferation, migration, and survival indicates an essential role in maintaining vascular integrity, while its regulation of vascular permeability and actin cytoskeletal dynamics suggests direct effects on vessel structure and responsiveness. Particularly relevant to hypertension is the annotation that VEGFA signaling is required for induction of NOS2 and NOS3 and thereby nitric oxide production in endothelial cells. Nitric oxide is a major vasodilator, and impaired endothelial nitric oxide bioavailability is a well-established mechanism contributing to increased vascular tone and elevated blood pressure. In parallel, activation of phosphoinositide three-kinase, protein kinase B, mitogen-activated protein kinase, extracellular signal-regulated kinase, SRC, and focal adhesion kinase pathways links VEGFA to adaptive or maladaptive vascular remodeling, which can influence arterial stiffness and microvascular rarefaction in hypertensive disease. The presence of soluble or decoy receptor isoforms that modulate VEGFA and VEGFC availability further suggests that altered signaling balance could affect lymphangiogenic and vascular responses relevant to fluid handling and pressure control. Overall, this protein appears highly relevant to hypertension because it integrates endothelial signaling, vasodilatory capacity, angiogenesis, and structural vascular adaptation.

    In parallel with oxidative stress, inflammatory chemokine signaling may provide an additional route through which the enriched protein set intersects with vascular dysfunction. CCL5 is of interest in hypertension primarily because its annotated signaling profile implicates inflammatory and calcium-dependent pathways that are highly relevant to vascular dysfunction. Chemokine signaling is increasingly understood to contribute to hypertension through recruitment and activation of immune cells, amplification of vascular inflammation, and promotion of remodeling in the vessel wall and target organs. The noted coupling to guanine nucleotide-binding protein subunit q proteins, inositol trisphosphate generation, and calcium mobilization is particularly notable, because intracellular calcium is a central regulator of vascular smooth muscle contraction and endothelial signaling. In addition, activation of phosphoinositide three-kinase, protein kinase B, and mitogen-activated protein kinase pathways suggests potential effects on cell survival, inflammatory activation, and structural remodeling. Although the annotation emphasizes neuronal survival and possible regulation of insulin secretion, the broader signaling architecture of this receptor is compatible with mechanisms implicated in hypertension, especially the inflammatory-endothelial axis and calcium-sensitive vascular responses. Thus, CCL5 may represent a plausible immunovascular contributor rather than a primary hemodynamic regulator.

    Shifting from inflammatory signaling to cellular stress responses, the following candidate may be more relevant to hypertensive tissue injury than to direct blood pressure regulation. CDKN1A is not a classical hypertension gene, but it is potentially relevant because vascular and renal injury in hypertension are strongly influenced by stress-induced cell cycle arrest, senescence, and maladaptive tissue remodeling. The annotated role of CDKN1A in deoxyribonucleic acid damage responses and growth arrest suggests that it may act as a molecular link between hemodynamic stress, oxidative injury, and altered cellular turnover in endothelial cells, vascular smooth muscle cells, or renal parenchymal cells. In chronic hypertension, repeated mechanical and oxidative stress can induce deoxyribonucleic acid damage and senescence-like programs, which in turn promote inflammation, fibrosis, and vascular stiffening. CDKN1A-mediated inhibition of proliferation may therefore be protective in some contexts by limiting uncontrolled remodeling, yet detrimental in others by favoring senescence and impaired tissue repair. This duality makes CDKN1A particularly interesting in relation to hypertensive target-organ damage rather than primary blood pressure control. Its functional annotation is supported by specific literature references documenting roles in G2 arrest and cyclin-cyclin-dependent kinase regulation. [222] [223] [224]

    A related but more indirect layer of relevance may arise from metabolic and redox adaptation, which brings attention to TALDO1. TALDO1 is potentially relevant to hypertension because pentose phosphate pathway activity is closely tied to cellular redox balance, nucleotide metabolism, and metabolic adaptation under stress. Although TALDO1 does not directly regulate vascular tone, its role in the pentose phosphate pathway suggests an indirect influence on oxidative stress handling and endothelial or renal cell resilience. Metabolic dysfunction and redox imbalance are major contributors to hypertension, particularly in cardiometabolic disease, and enzymes that shape these pathways may affect susceptibility to vascular injury. The annotation that TALDO1 can alter other metabolic pathways through changes in subcellular localization further raises the possibility that it participates in broader stress responses. Therefore, TALDO1 is best considered a secondary or contextual hypertension-related protein, especially in settings where metabolic syndrome, oxidative stress, or endothelial dysfunction are prominent. [225] [226]

    Finally, extending from metabolic and vascular mechanisms to neuroimmune regulation, CRLF1 may represent a more context-dependent candidate. CRLF1 has a less direct connection to hypertension than VEGFA or SOD2, but it may still be of interest because neuroimmune mechanisms contribute to blood pressure regulation. Its role in a neurotropic cytokine complex suggests potential relevance to autonomic or sensory neural pathways that influence cardiovascular homeostasis, while its possible immune regulatory function could intersect with inflammatory components of hypertension. However, based on the provided annotation, the evidence is currently more suggestive than definitive. CRLF1 would therefore be considered a lower-priority candidate whose importance may depend on specific disease contexts involving neuroimmune dysregulation rather than core vascular mechanisms of hypertension.

    6. Neutrophil degranulation (REAC:R-HSA-6798695)

    Agent Summary: Neutrophil degranulation is a critical immune response mechanism where neutrophils release granule contents, including proteases and oxidant-generating enzymes, to combat pathogens and influence tissue dynamics. Pathway members (enrichment overlap): A1BG, ACAA1, ADA2, ANPEP, ARSA, ARSB. Context proteins (upstream regulators / disease context, not direct members): CRELD1, LTBP2, LTBP3, TGFB1. [155] [156] [157]
    Read Context ▽

    Neutrophil degranulation is a core effector program of innate immunity in which activated neutrophils rapidly mobilize and release the contents of distinct intracellular granule compartments into the extracellular space or onto the cell surface. These granules contain proteases, oxidant-generating enzymes, antimicrobial peptides, matrix-remodeling enzymes, adhesion-related molecules, and inflammatory mediators. Through this process, neutrophils can eliminate pathogens, amplify leukocyte recruitment, remodel extracellular matrix, alter endothelial barrier properties, and shape tissue repair. The biological consequences of neutrophil degranulation depend on the intensity, timing, and tissue context of release. Controlled degranulation contributes to host defense and resolution of injury, whereas excessive or chronic degranulation promotes oxidative stress, proteolytic tissue damage, endothelial dysfunction, thrombogenicity, and maladaptive vascular remodeling. The cited literature highlights representative granule products such as myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinase eight, matrix metalloproteinase nine, neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin, cathelicidin, arginase, and azurocidin, all of which can influence vascular tone, nitric oxide bioavailability, extracellular matrix integrity, and inflammatory signaling. In cardiovascular and inflammatory disorders, neutrophil degranulation is increasingly viewed not merely as a marker of immune activation but as a mechanistically relevant contributor to organ injury and remodeling.

    Against this biological background, the collected publications support a substantive, although still context-dependent, link between neutrophil degranulation and hypertension by indicating that neutrophil activation, granule release, and closely related extracellular trap formation participate in vascular injury, endothelial dysfunction, inflammatory amplification, and tissue remodeling that may sustain elevated blood pressure and hypertensive organ damage. Direct evidence comes from pulmonary vascular disease models, where inhibition of neutrophil activation reduced lung myeloperoxidase activity, used as an index of neutrophil degranulation, and prevented acute pulmonary artery hypertension after protamine exposure, suggesting that neutrophil degranulation can occur upstream of pressure elevation in the pulmonary circulation. Consistently, transcriptomic analysis in pulmonary arterial hypertension identified enrichment of neutrophil degranulation among disease-associated pathways, and an experimental rat study of monocrotaline-induced pulmonary arterial hypertension showed increased secretory degranulation early in disease and progressive myeloperoxidase release with oxidant stress during later stages, supporting a possible role in pulmonary vascular remodeling and progression. Evidence also extends to systemic hypertension. A large proteomic risk prediction study for incident hypertension identified neutrophil degranulation as one of the principal enriched biological pathways, suggesting that this pathway may be active before or during the transition to overt disease. Clinical observations further show that inflammatory cell signatures related to neutrophils are heightened in specific hypertensive phenotypes, as patients with non-dipping hypertension displayed elevated neutrophil-related inflammatory ratios, while another study demonstrated altered neutrophil subpopulations in arterial hypertension with fewer cytoplasmic granules together with increased reactive oxygen species production, a pattern compatible with prior or ongoing degranulation. Mechanistically, the literature indicates several routes through which degranulation may promote hypertension: released proteases and oxidant enzymes can damage the endothelium, reduce nitric oxide signaling, increase vascular stiffness, and remodel extracellular matrix; myeloperoxidase-driven oxidant chemistry can intensify halogenating stress; and degranulation is closely coupled to extracellular trap formation, which has been reviewed as a contributor to hypertension and target-organ injury. Experimental work presented in a hypertension model further showed that inability to efficiently form extracellular traps attenuated angiotensin-induced hypertension and improved vascular reactivity, while hypertensive stretch augmented extracellular trap formation, thereby linking neutrophil effector activation to vascular dysfunction. Additional support comes from pregnancy-induced hypertension, in which circulating neutrophil elastase was elevated and proposed to contribute to vascular lesions. Taken together, these studies suggest that neutrophil degranulation is not only an inflammatory correlate of hypertension but also a plausible pathogenic mechanism connecting immune activation to endothelial injury, oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodeling, abnormal vascular reactivity, and progression of both pulmonary and systemic hypertensive disease. [155] [156] [157] [158] [159] [160] [161] [162]

    This literature-based interpretation is further supported by the pathway enrichment result. There were 67 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of neutrophil degranulation, indicating a substantial convergence of hypertension-related molecular signals on an innate immune effector process that governs protease release, oxidant generation, extracellular matrix remodeling, endothelial barrier regulation, and inflammatory amplification. The size of this enriched protein set, comprising 67 proteins, supports the interpretation that neutrophil degranulation is not a marginal finding but a quantitatively prominent functional theme in hypertension, consistent with the concept that excessive granule cargo release can contribute to oxidative stress, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, vascular injury, thrombogenicity, and maladaptive remodeling of the vessel wall. In this context, representative granule-associated mediators described for this pathway, including myeloperoxidase, neutrophil elastase, matrix metalloproteinase eight, matrix metalloproteinase nine, neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin, cathelicidin, arginase, and azurocidin, provide biologically plausible links between immune activation and the hemodynamic, endothelial, and structural abnormalities that characterize hypertension.

    To place these 67 proteins into a systems-level context, the interaction network is shown below. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 67 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link for further inspection of network connectivity and functional relationships.

    CD14 is among the most compelling hypertension-relevant proteins in this list because it sits at the interface between innate immune sensing, vascular inflammation, and lipid-driven inflammatory signaling. Chronic low-grade inflammation is now recognized as a central contributor to hypertension, particularly through endothelial dysfunction, vascular remodeling, and enhanced cytokine production. By promoting Toll-like receptor four and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells-dependent inflammatory activation in response to lipopolysaccharide, and potentially mediating inflammatory responses to modified low-density lipoprotein, CD14 may contribute to the sterile and microbial inflammatory signals that exacerbate vascular stiffness and impair vasodilatory homeostasis. These functions are especially relevant in hypertension associated with metabolic dysfunction, obesity, or vascular injury, where innate immune activation amplifies arterial inflammation and target-organ damage. [163] [164] [165] [166]

    A closely related theme is extracellular matrix signaling and fibrotic remodeling, which brings attention to integrin subunit alpha V. ITGAV stands out because of its direct connection to extracellular matrix signaling, vascular remodeling, and transforming growth factor beta activation, all of which are highly relevant to hypertension pathogenesis. Transforming growth factor beta signaling is a major driver of vascular fibrosis, arterial stiffening, and renal injury, which are hallmarks of chronic hypertension and hypertensive end-organ damage. Through its role in activating latent transforming growth factor beta one, ITGAV-containing integrins may facilitate profibrotic signaling in the vasculature and kidney. In addition, alpha-V integrins participate in angiogenesis, endothelial-matrix interactions, and inflammatory signaling, suggesting that dysregulation of ITGAV could influence both structural and signaling components of elevated blood pressure. This makes ITGAV particularly relevant to mechanisms linking matrix remodeling with persistent increases in vascular resistance. [167] [168] [169] [170] [171]

    In parallel with matrix remodeling, maintenance of endothelial structure is also likely to be important in this pathway context. PTPRB is highly relevant to hypertension because endothelial integrity is fundamental to vascular tone regulation, barrier function, and resistance vessel remodeling. Hypertension is strongly associated with endothelial dysfunction, including altered junctional stability, increased permeability, and impaired nitric oxide-dependent signaling. A protein that helps maintain endothelial polarity, lumen formation, and cell-cell junction organization could plausibly influence vascular responsiveness and microvascular health. Dysfunction in these processes may promote vascular rarefaction, inflammation, and stiffness, thereby contributing to increased peripheral resistance and hypertensive target-organ injury. Thus, PTPRB is notable as a vascular homeostasis regulator with mechanistic relevance to blood pressure control. [172] [173] [174] [175] [176]

    Beyond endothelial regulation, metabolic inflammation may offer another route through which this pathway intersects with hypertension. FABP5 is of particular interest in hypertension because it connects lipid handling, inflammatory signaling, and transcriptional control. Hypertension frequently coexists with obesity, insulin resistance, and altered fatty acid metabolism, and these metabolic disturbances can drive vascular inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. FABP5-mediated transport of fatty acids and retinoic acid to nuclear receptors may reshape gene programs involved in vascular cell survival, inflammation, and remodeling. Its reported role in nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation and prostaglandin E2 biosynthesis further strengthens its relevance, as inflammatory lipid mediators contribute to vascular dysfunction and renal sodium-handling abnormalities. FABP5 may therefore represent a mechanistic bridge between metabolic inflammation and hypertensive vascular disease. [177] [178] [179] [180] [181]

    Immune restraint mechanisms may be equally informative, particularly where persistent inflammation sustains vascular injury. LAIR1 is relevant to hypertension because immune dysregulation is increasingly recognized as a driver of blood pressure elevation and end-organ damage. T cells, innate immune cells, and inflammatory cytokines contribute to vascular dysfunction, renal inflammation, and fibrosis in experimental and human hypertension. As a broad inhibitory checkpoint receptor, LAIR1 may restrain these pathogenic immune responses by limiting calcium signaling, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation, and inflammatory cytokine output. Reduced inhibitory signaling through pathways such as LAIR1 could therefore favor chronic vascular inflammation and hypertensive remodeling, whereas preserved LAIR1 activity may be protective. Its importance lies less in direct hemodynamic control and more in modulation of the inflammatory milieu that sustains hypertension. [182] [183] [184]

    A similar immunoregulatory perspective applies to CD300A, which may act as another brake on excessive innate immune activation. CD300A is noteworthy because it suppresses innate immune activation, particularly myeloid differentiation primary response eighty-eight-dependent Toll-like receptor signaling, a pathway with broad relevance to vascular inflammation and hypertension. Excessive Toll-like receptor-driven cytokine production can impair endothelial function, enhance oxidative stress, and promote vascular remodeling. By acting as a brake on these pathways, CD300A may influence the intensity of inflammatory responses that contribute to elevated blood pressure. Its role in mast cell regulation is also potentially relevant, as mast cell-derived mediators can affect vascular permeability, fibrosis, and local inflammatory tone. Overall, CD300A emerges as a plausible protective modulator in hypertension-associated immune activation. [182] [183] [184]

    In addition to these inhibitory immune receptors, interferon-associated and matrix-regulatory proteins may further broaden the inflammatory context of this pathway. BST2 is not a classic hypertension gene, but it is potentially relevant because it links interferon signaling, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activity, matrix remodeling, and cell surface protease regulation. Interferon-driven immune activation and chronic inflammatory signaling can contribute to endothelial dysfunction and vascular injury, especially in inflammatory or infection-associated cardiovascular states. The reported inhibition of matrix metalloproteinase fourteen and matrix metalloproteinase fifteen-related pathways is also notable, since matrix metalloproteinases influence extracellular matrix turnover, vascular remodeling, and arterial stiffness. BST2 may therefore be most relevant in secondary or inflammation-associated hypertension, where persistent immune activation and altered matrix regulation contribute to vascular pathology. [185] [186] [187] [188] [189] [190] [191] [192] [193] [194] [195] [196] [197] [198]

    Another potentially relevant inflammatory mechanism involves nucleic acid sensing and mitochondrial stress. RNASET2 is of interest for hypertension primarily through its role in innate immune activation and mitochondrial ribonucleic acid handling. Toll-like receptor seven and Toll-like receptor eight-linked inflammatory pathways can amplify cytokine production and contribute to vascular and renal inflammation. In addition, mitochondrial dysfunction and release of mitochondrial nucleic acids are increasingly implicated in sterile inflammation, oxidative stress, and endothelial injury, all of which are relevant to hypertension. By controlling both microbial and mitochondrial ribonucleic acid processing, RNASET2 could influence the generation of immunostimulatory ligands that shape chronic inflammatory states. This makes it a plausible contributor to hypertension in contexts where innate immune activation and mitochondrial stress are prominent. [199] [200] [201] [202] [203]

    Lipid trafficking provides an additional angle from which hypertension-related vascular injury may be considered. NPC2 is potentially relevant to hypertension because disturbed cholesterol trafficking and sterol homeostasis can contribute to vascular inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and atherosclerotic remodeling, all of which worsen arterial stiffness and cardiovascular risk in hypertensive individuals. Although NPC2 is more directly linked to lysosomal lipid transport than to blood pressure regulation itself, altered intracellular cholesterol handling can affect membrane composition, signaling platforms, and inflammatory responses in vascular and immune cells. Its role is therefore most meaningful in the broader context of cardiometabolic hypertension, where dyslipidemia and vascular injury coexist. [204] [205] [206] [207]

    Related to this metabolic perspective, peroxisomal lipid oxidation may also influence vascular and inflammatory homeostasis. ACAA1 is relevant to hypertension because peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation is closely linked to systemic metabolic health, oxidative balance, and lipid-derived signaling. Impaired fatty acid catabolism can promote accumulation of bioactive lipid species that contribute to endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and insulin resistance, all of which are recognized contributors to hypertension. Although the connection is indirect, ACAA1 may be particularly important in metabolic forms of hypertension where altered lipid oxidation and redox stress influence vascular tone and organ injury. [208] [209]

    Shifting from metabolism to structural remodeling, extracellular matrix composition remains another plausible contributor to elevated vascular resistance. CANT1 is noteworthy because proteoglycan synthesis is a key determinant of extracellular matrix composition and vascular wall structure. In hypertension, remodeling of the vascular extracellular matrix contributes to increased stiffness, reduced compliance, and altered mechanotransduction. A protein involved in proteoglycan biosynthesis could therefore influence arterial wall properties and susceptibility to hypertensive remodeling. While the link is less direct than for inflammatory or endothelial regulators, CANT1 may have relevance to the structural component of hypertension pathogenesis.

    Finally, protein folding stress and metabolic dysfunction may offer one more mechanistic layer relevant to vascular disease. TXNDC5 may be relevant to hypertension through mechanisms involving endoplasmic reticulum stress, protein folding homeostasis, and metabolic dysfunction. Endoplasmic reticulum stress is increasingly implicated in endothelial dysfunction, vascular inflammation, and impaired insulin signaling, each of which can contribute to hypertension. As a protein disulfide isomerase, TXNDC5 may affect the maturation of secreted and membrane proteins involved in vascular signaling or inflammatory responses. Its ability to reduce insulin disulfide bonds also suggests a potential connection to insulin resistance, a common comorbidity that promotes hypertensive cardiovascular disease. [210] [211]

    7. Overview of proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators (WP:WP5095)

    Agent Summary: The 'Overview of proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators' pathway in hypertension describes a complex biological network that integrates immune activation, neurohormonal signaling, mechanical stress, and extracellular matrix remodeling. Pathway members (enrichment overlap): AREG, CCL14, CCL15, CCL16, CCL18, CCL20. Context proteins (upstream regulators / disease context, not direct members): EGFR, NOS3. [100] [101] [102]
    Read Context ▽

    The pathway described as an overview of proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators represents a convergent biological network that links immune activation, neurohormonal signaling, mechanical stress, cellular activation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. In this pathway, proinflammatory mediators such as cytokines and related signaling molecules promote the recruitment and activation of inflammatory and stromal cells, while profibrotic mediators such as growth factors and hormone-dependent signals stimulate fibroblast activation, myofibroblast transition, collagen synthesis, and structural remodeling of tissues. The publications provided suggest that this pathway is strongly influenced by pressure overload and by excessive activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. In the cardiovascular setting, increased mechanical stress and inflammatory signaling activate fibroblasts and induce intracellular signaling pathways, especially mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, which enhances extracellular matrix production and tissue stiffening. In the kidney, angiotensin two and aldosterone act not only as regulators of vascular tone and salt-water balance but also as direct proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators that damage the vascular endothelium, glomerulus, and renal interstitium. Taken together, this pathway may be understood as a disease-amplifying axis in which hemodynamic stress, inflammatory mediators, and fibrotic signaling reinforce one another, potentially leading to maladaptive remodeling in the heart, vasculature, and kidney.

    This broader mechanistic framework provides a useful basis for understanding why the pathway appears closely related to hypertension. Hypertension both activates and is sustained by proinflammatory and profibrotic signaling across multiple organs. One publication shows that pressure overload increases levels of proinflammatory cytokines, profibrotic growth factors, and mechanical stimulation, which activate cardiac fibroblasts, trigger mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, and promote extracellular matrix synthesis and remodeling; although initially adaptive, this fibrotic response ultimately increases myocardial stiffness and impairs ventricular function, illustrating how elevated pressure can be translated into structural heart disease in hypertensive states [100]. A second publication demonstrates that excessive activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system promotes systemic and glomerular capillary hypertension and, beyond its hemodynamic actions, directly drives inflammation and fibrosis through angiotensin two and aldosterone, thereby injuring the vascular endothelium and kidney tissue [101]. Taken together, these studies support a unified model in which hypertension is not simply a disorder of elevated blood pressure, but a chronic pathological condition in which neurohormonal activation, inflammatory signaling, and fibrotic remodeling interact to damage target organs. In this context, proinflammatory and profibrotic mediators may contribute to vascular dysfunction, renal injury, cardiac stiffening, and progressive end-organ remodeling, while these structural changes may in turn further worsen blood pressure regulation, thereby creating a self-perpetuating cycle of hypertensive disease. [100] [101]

    To further illustrate the organization of this enriched protein set, the network representation is shown below. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 39 proteins, together with the link to the STRING webpage for interactive inspection of the network topology and connectivity relationships.

    Extending from endothelial regulation to cardiometabolic adaptation, EPO also appears potentially relevant within this dataset. EPO stands out because several of its reported functions intersect with mechanisms relevant to hypertension and hypertensive end-organ damage, particularly in the cardiovascular and metabolic systems. Most notably, EPO inhibits apoptosis and inflammatory responses in cardiomyocytes through AKT pathway activation [102], suggesting a potential protective role in the myocardium under hemodynamic stress. Since chronic hypertension promotes cardiac remodeling, inflammation, and myocyte injury, this anti-apoptotic signaling is mechanistically important. In addition, its effects on hepatocyte autophagy and lipid uptake [103] [104] connect EPO to systemic metabolic regulation, which is highly relevant because metabolic dysfunction frequently coexists with hypertension and worsens vascular disease. Its endocrine role in iron homeostasis after blood loss [105] [106] [107] [108] may be less directly linked to blood pressure itself, but altered erythropoietic and iron-regulatory states can influence blood viscosity, tissue oxygenation, and cardiovascular strain. Collectively, the strongest hypertension-related implication of EPO in this dataset is its modulation of cardiomyocyte survival and inflammatory signaling, with additional relevance through metabolic and systemic homeostatic pathways. [105] [106] [107] [108] [103] [102] [104]

    A related remodeling-oriented perspective may also be considered for AREG. AREG is potentially relevant to hypertension because EGFR ligand signaling is strongly associated with cellular growth, proliferation, and tissue remodeling. Although the description provided here is concise, its mitogenic activity in fibroblasts is especially noteworthy in the setting of hypertension, where vascular and cardiac fibrosis are major determinants of disease progression and target-organ damage. EGFR pathway activation has been broadly implicated in vascular smooth muscle activation, fibroblast proliferation, and maladaptive remodeling, all of which contribute to increased vascular stiffness and elevated peripheral resistance. Thus, AREG may represent a plausible mediator of hypertensive remodeling, particularly through autocrine and paracrine growth-promoting effects in stromal and mesenchymal cell populations.

    In parallel with growth factor-driven remodeling, inflammatory cytokine signaling may provide another layer of relevance. IL17C is relevant to hypertension because chronic low-grade inflammation is increasingly recognized as a major contributor to vascular dysfunction, endothelial injury, and hypertensive end-organ damage. The function described here emphasizes activation of NF-kappa-B and MAPK pathways and synergy with TNF and IL1B, which are canonical inflammatory axes implicated in vascular inflammation and remodeling. Although IL17C is primarily characterized as an epithelial cytokine, its ability to amplify inflammatory programs suggests a plausible role in systemic inflammatory states that predispose to or exacerbate hypertension. The note that enhanced IL17C/IL17RE signaling may increase susceptibility to autoimmune disease further strengthens its relevance, as immune dysregulation and cytokine-driven inflammation are increasingly linked to resistant and organ-damaging forms of hypertension.

    By contrast, IL19 may be interpreted somewhat differently, as its reported functions suggest a potentially counter-regulatory role. IL19 is notable because it combines anti-inflammatory and proangiogenic properties, both of which may be meaningful in hypertension. Its capacity to polarize immunity toward a Th2 phenotype and suppress IFN-gamma [109] suggests a counter-regulatory role against pro-inflammatory immune activation, a known driver of endothelial dysfunction and vascular injury in hypertension. In addition, proangiogenic signaling and activation of JAK-STAT, especially STAT3 [110], may influence vascular adaptation and tissue repair. Depending on context, such effects could be beneficial by limiting inflammatory vascular damage, although persistent STAT3-associated signaling can also participate in remodeling responses. Therefore, IL19 may be interpreted as a potentially protective immunoregulatory cytokine within hypertensive disease biology, particularly where inflammation contributes to progression. [111] [109] [112] [110]

    Another potentially relevant inflammatory component is CCL5-related signaling, although its connection appears somewhat more indirect. CCL5-related signaling may have a meaningful, albeit somewhat indirect, connection to hypertension through inflammatory chemokine biology and calcium-dependent signal transduction. The described receptor function includes calcium mobilization and activation of PI3K-AKT and MAP kinase pathways, which are broadly relevant to vascular cell activation and inflammatory responses. In addition, the reported connection to insulin secretion suggests a link to metabolic regulation, and metabolic dysfunction is a major comorbidity that promotes hypertension. While the annotation provided here emphasizes neuronal and pancreatic effects rather than direct vascular actions, chemokine pathways such as CCL5 are frequently implicated in leukocyte recruitment and vascular inflammation, making this axis potentially relevant to hypertensive vascular injury and metabolic-cardiovascular crosstalk.

    Finally, IL12B may add a complementary perspective centered on oxidative stress control and cellular stress responses. Although IL12B is not as directly connected to blood pressure regulation as VEGFA or EPO, the functions listed suggest relevance to hypertension through oxidative stress, innate immunity, and autophagy. Oxidative stress and defective proteostasis are well-established contributors to endothelial dysfunction, vascular stiffness, and hypertensive organ injury. In particular, activation of the KEAP1-NRF2 antioxidant pathway and regulation of inflammatory signaling [113] [114] may influence how vascular and immune cells respond to chronic stress. Because hypertension is increasingly understood as a disorder involving immune activation and redox imbalance, proteins that coordinate autophagy and antioxidant defense may have mechanistic importance, especially in the progression of vascular and renal damage. [113] [114]

    8. Spinal cord injury (WP:WP2431)

    Agent Summary: Spinal cord injury disrupts autonomic control over cardiovascular functions, leading to chronic autonomic instability and hypertension due to the interruption of supraspinal inhibitory control over sympathetic circuits. Pathway members (enrichment overlap): BCAN, CXCL10, EGFR, ICAM1, IL1R1, IL6. Context proteins (upstream regulators / disease context, not direct members): CD40, EDA2R, FASLG, LTBR, NOS3. [90] [91] [92]
    Read Context ▽

    Spinal cord injury is a pathological state initiated by traumatic or perioperative damage to the spinal cord, followed by persistent neurological, vascular, immune, endocrine, and metabolic consequences. In the context of cardiovascular regulation, the spinal cord is not merely a conduit for descending motor and sensory signals, but also a critical integrative structure for autonomic control of vascular tone, cardiac function, and reflex blood pressure regulation. Injury, particularly at or above the major thoracic sympathetic outflow, interrupts supraspinal inhibitory and modulatory control over sympathetic preganglionic circuits. This disruption produces a chronic state of autonomic instability in which patients may experience both sustained blood pressure abnormalities and episodic hypertensive crises triggered by otherwise innocuous stimuli below the lesion, such as bladder distension, bowel care, pain, or clinical urodynamic testing. Experimental studies further indicate that spinal cord injury induces maladaptive structural and functional plasticity within spinal sympathetic networks, including excitatory interneuron remodeling, enhanced noradrenergic signaling, and inflammatory signaling driven in part by soluble tumor necrosis factor alpha, all of which may amplify sympathetic reflexes and promote pathological pressor responses. In parallel, spinal cord injury is associated with broader cardiometabolic dysregulation, including adipose tissue dysfunction, abnormal lipolysis, ectopic lipid deposition, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia, which may contribute to long-term vascular risk. Clinical cohort data further indicate that traumatic spinal cord injury is associated with increased long-term incidence of hypertension, stroke, and coronary artery disease, supporting the view that spinal cord injury is a systemic disease state with substantial relevance to blood pressure control and hypertensive vascular injury.

    To extend this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment analysis provides a complementary molecular view of how this pathway may relate to hypertension. There were 19 hypertension-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing spinal cord injury as a pathological state that disrupts autonomic cardiovascular regulation, vascular control, immune signaling, endocrine balance, and metabolic homeostasis, thereby linking traumatic or perioperative spinal cord damage to sustained blood pressure dysregulation, episodic hypertensive responses, and increased long-term vascular risk. This enrichment profile is quantitatively notable because it captures a 19-protein disease-relevant functional module centered on mechanisms directly pertinent to hypertension, including altered sympathetic signaling, exaggerated pressor reflexes, inflammatory remodeling, and cardiometabolic disturbance, all of which are described as contributing to elevated blood pressure burden, hypertensive crises, stroke risk, and coronary artery disease in the pathway annotation. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 19 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link.

    A related but somewhat different line of reasoning concerns proteins involved in structural remodeling of the vascular wall. MMP12 is potentially relevant to hypertension because extracellular matrix remodeling and large-artery stiffening are major determinants of elevated systolic blood pressure and hypertensive target-organ damage. Its significant elastolytic activity is particularly notable, as degradation of elastic fiber components can reduce arterial compliance and promote vascular stiffening, a hallmark of aging-associated and inflammation-associated hypertension. Beyond direct matrix degradation, MMP12 may participate in inflammatory vascular remodeling, which contributes to resistance vessel dysfunction, altered pulse-wave propagation, and maladaptive cardiac and renal changes. Although MMP12 is not among the canonical blood pressure genes, its function aligns closely with structural mechanisms that may sustain or worsen hypertension, especially in contexts of chronic inflammation, vascular injury, or remodeling of the arterial wall.

    In contrast to these more established vascular and renal mechanisms, some candidates may be relevant through signaling systems that bridge neural and cardiovascular biology. RGMA is an intriguing candidate in relation to hypertension because its biology intersects with two pathways that are highly relevant to cardiovascular disease: RHOA-ROCK signaling and bone morphogenetic protein-associated signaling. The RHOA-ROCK pathway is strongly implicated in vasoconstriction, vascular smooth muscle contractility, endothelial dysfunction, and vascular remodeling, all of which contribute to hypertension. Although the function provided here emphasizes neuronal growth cone collapse and neurite inhibition, the signaling architecture suggests a broader relevance to cytoskeletal regulation and tissue remodeling. Its additional role as a bone morphogenetic protein coreceptor is also noteworthy, as bone morphogenetic protein and transforming growth factor beta family signaling has recognized roles in vascular homeostasis, inflammation, and remodeling. Thus, RGMA may be relevant not because it is a classic hypertension effector, but because it connects neurodevelopmental guidance mechanisms with signaling modules known to influence vascular tone and structural adaptation in hypertensive disease.

    This emphasis on neural organization also provides a natural transition to extracellular matrix proteins that may shape autonomic circuitry more indirectly. BCAN has a more indirect but still potentially meaningful connection to hypertension through the central nervous system regulation of blood pressure. Because it contributes to the organization and stabilization of the neural extracellular matrix, BCAN may influence neuronal connectivity, synaptic microenvironments, and signaling within brain regions involved in autonomic cardiovascular control. Hypertension is increasingly understood to involve central neuroplastic and neuroinflammatory mechanisms, particularly within hypothalamic and brainstem circuits that regulate sympathetic outflow. Although there is no direct indication here that BCAN controls vascular function, its role in maintaining the mature nervous system extracellular environment suggests a plausible link to neurogenic components of hypertension. This makes BCAN more speculative than NOS1, but still of interest if the biological context involves central autonomic regulation.

    A closely related interpretation may also apply to NCAN, which appears most plausibly connected to hypertension through neurodevelopmental and neuroregulatory mechanisms rather than direct vascular actions. By modulating neuronal adhesion, neurite growth, and extracellular matrix interactions, NCAN may influence the formation or maintenance of neural circuits that govern autonomic balance. Since sympathetic overactivity is a major driver of many forms of hypertension, proteins that shape neuronal connectivity may have indirect relevance to disease susceptibility or progression. However, compared with NOS1 or MMP12, the current functional description supports only a relatively indirect association. NCAN may therefore be best regarded as a secondary candidate whose importance would depend on whether the disease model emphasizes central nervous system remodeling, autonomic dysregulation, or extracellular matrix changes in neural tissues.
